a32.speaker: Jeremiah Manele, Solomon Islands Prime Minister
a32.speech: Said that 21 donor countries, including the United States and China, will not be invited to the region's top political meeting, a move that follows pressure from Beijing to exclude Taiwan. ; Told the Solomon Islands parliament his cabinet had decided no dialogue partners would be invited to this year's event, because a review of each country's relationship with the Pacific had not been completed. ; Said he had informed the forum's 18 leaders of the decision; the World Bank, the Asia Development Bank and civil society groups would attend, he added.

a32.speaker: US State Department spokesperson
a32.speech: "disappointed by reports that Solomon Islands has decided to exclude dialogue and development partners from the PIF Leaders Meeting this year." ; "We support the continued attendance of all PIF partners, including Taiwan, at the annual PIF Leaders Meeting, as previously agreed by PIF leaders in 1992."

a32.speaker: Peter Kenilorea Jr, Opposition politician and chairman of parliament's foreign relations committee
a32.speech: Said the decision was "a massive missed opportunity" for Pacific Island countries to meet global donors. ; "We know this issue is all about China and Taiwan," he told parliament. ; Said he feared China, which has a strong presence in the Solomon Islands, would hold bilateral meetings with Pacific leaders on the margins of the forum regardless. ; "This could be seen by some PIF leaders as a betrayal of the collective and could risk an even bigger rift of the group," he said in comments to Reuters.

a32.speaker: Hilda Heine, Marshall Islands President
a32.speech: Criticised interference in the forum's affairs in a speech to the Taiwan ally's parliament, saying China had "interfered" at last year's meeting in Tonga to change the language of the leaders' communique; references to Taiwan were removed after Chinese diplomats complained.

a275.speaker: Jessica Long, US Embassy Charge d'Affaires in Namibia
a275.speech: revealed that the United States of America has listed Namibia among the six countries to share strategies on epidemic control measures with other countries, following a courtesy call on President Hage Geingob at State House ; while commending the government for its commitment to epidemic control, says Namibia can now share its lessons with others.

a275.speaker: Jessica Long, US Embassy Charge d'Affaires in Namibia
a275.speech: The US diplomat also discussed the upcoming US-Africa summit and the interests of US businesses in investing in Namibia.

a275.speaker: Hage Geingob, President of Namibia
a275.speech: commended the US government, especially the George W. Bush administration, for helping to address socio-economic challenges through the Millennium Challenge Account program.

a275.speaker: Government of Namibia
a275.speech: has described the upper-middle income status classification by the World Bank as unfair.

a494.speaker: Kagiso Mmusi, Minister of Defence, Justice and Security
a494.speech: Announced that the State seeks to formalise the collection of information through undercover means ; tabled the Criminal Procedure and Evidence (controlled investigation) Bill on urgency, a move that sparked debates as to what the government's intention is with a Bill meant for interception of communication supposedly for investigative purposes.

a738.speaker: Kevin Watkins, former CEO of Save the Children UK (commentary provided by Project Syndicate)
a738.speech: Writes that the UK now finds itself embroiled in a new political order that prioritises defence spending over aid, calling for a reevaluation of global cooperation; argues that a Labour government has torn up the remnants of the bipartisan aid consensus, joined a global attack on aid, and set a course that will leave the UK among the world's least generous countries, illustrating the political forces shaping a new world order, notably US President Donald Trump's view of international cooperation as a zero-sum game played by losers.

a738.speaker: Kevin Watkins, former CEO of Save the Children UK (commentary provided by Project Syndicate)
a738.speech: Argues that the priority is to minimise harm: maintaining the UK's 2.6 billion dollars commitment to the World Bank's International Development Association is critical because every dollar contributed can leverage three to four dollars of financial support for the poorest countries; that the UK could channel more humanitarian aid through local actors rather than bureaucratic UN agencies; that there is a strong argument to protect spending on life-saving programs such as child nutrition, vaccinations, and HIV/AIDS, and to minimise cuts in areas where the UK is a global frontrunner, like girls' education and social protection; that Starmer's government could demand comprehensive debt relief at the UN International Conference on Financing for Development; and that political leaders in the UK and across the West need to communicate the hard truth that global challenges like climate change, war, and poverty require international cooperation.

a738.speaker: David Cameron, then UK Prime Minister
a738.speech: Stood before the United Nations General Assembly in 2015 and challenged other donor countries to follow the UK's lead and back the newly minted Sustainable Development Goals for eradicating poverty with their aid money: "We haven't just achieved the UN's 0.7pc [aid-to-GNI spending] target, we've enshrined it in law."

a738.speaker: Keir Starmer, British Prime Minister
a738.speech: Announced the decision to cut foreign aid and channel the savings to an expanded defence budget ahead of a meeting with Trump, with the aid budget set to fall from 0.5pc to 0.3pc of GNI, the lowest level since the late 1990s; now cites Russian security threats to justify deeper cuts.

a738.speaker: Kemi Badenoch, Conservative leader
a738.speech: Applauded the decision to convert ODA into defence spending.

a738.speaker: Reform UK party (election manifesto)
a738.speech: Called for the aid budget to be halved.

a738.speaker: Jenny Chapman, Britain's development minister
a738.speech: Told a parliamentary committee in May that "the days of viewing the UK government as a global charity are over."

a738.speaker: A recent study (cited)
a738.speech: Found that Trump's suspension of aid could result in 14 million additional deaths, including 4.5 million children under five, by 2030.

a738.speaker: Boris Johnson, then UK Prime Minister
a738.speech: "Temporarily" reduced foreign aid to 0.5pc of GNI, citing the COVID-19 crisis, after making the ill-judged decision to fold the Department for International Development into the Foreign & Commonwealth Office.

a738.speaker: David Lammy, UK Foreign Secretary
a738.speech: Described the decimation of the aid budget as an exercise in "progressive realism."

a1056.speaker: Mai Mala Buni, Yobe State Governor
a1056.speech: Reiterated the state's shared commitment to implement durable solutions, acknowledging the vital support and collaborative efforts of the international community in fostering sustainable development and lasting peace in Northeast Nigeria: "On behalf of the government and people of Yobe State, l extend our deep appreciation for the continuous support, expertise, and critical role played by the international partners in achieving peace and development."

a1056.speaker: Mai Mala Buni, Yobe State Governor
a1056.speech: Enumerated the ongoing efforts and commitments to addressing some development gaps, particularly in healthcare, education, agriculture, public infrastructure, and water facilities, assuring the readiness of his administration to create sustainable conditions that would support voluntary, safe, and dignified pathways for internally displaced persons (IDPs) within the state.

a1056.speaker: Mai Mala Buni, Yobe State Governor
a1056.speech: Announced the constitution of a resource mobilization team under his leadership and other key members, to drive the state's resource mobilization efforts, and appealed for support through linkages and networking with Geneva and other international donors.

a1056.speaker: Baba Mallam Wali, Secretary to the Yobe State Government
a1056.speech: In his remarks, highlighted the critical role played by the international community and development partners in supporting Yobe State's development aspirations, commending the Governor for providing the political will and leadership drive to achieve the sustainable development goals.

a1056.speaker: Suleiman Dauda, Yobe State SOLID Focal Person and Project Coordinator
a1056.speech: Said the commitment of the governor provides effective, efficient, and workable solutions to the management of displacement in the state, and said the existing state policies and development goals focusing on health, education, agriculture, livelihood, economic growth, human rights, security and safety of vulnerable populations places Yobe State on the same page with the State Action Plan.

a1056.speaker: Diplomats representing various countries and donor organizations
a1056.speech: Expressed their readiness to partner Yobe state government to achieve durable solutions in a coordinated manner, applauding the state's unique position as the only Nigerian state with a domesticated State IDP policy, and State Action Plan on Durable Solutions.

a1091.speaker: US government (sanctions notice)
a1091.speech: Accused Defence Minister Colonel Sadio Camara, Air Force Chief of Staff Colonel Alou Boi Diarra and Deputy Chief of Staff Lieutenant Colonel Adama Bagayoko of "having materially assisted, sponsored or provided financial, material or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, the Wagner Group" ; said the three men were instrumental in capacitating the paramilitary organisation to assert its influence in Mali since December 2021, and that since then the number of civilians killed in operations conducted by the Wagner Group alongside the Malian Armed Forces has risen to alarming levels.

a1091.speaker: Antony Blinken, US Secretary of State
a1091.speech: "Civilian fatalities have surged by 278% since Wagner forces were deployed to Mali in December 2021," said in a notice.

a1091.speaker: US government
a1091.speech: Said it was its mandate as the largest bilateral donor of development and humanitarian assistance to Mali to "take action against those who facilitate the Wagner Group's destabilising activities, which pose threats to peace and security in Mali and the region."

a1091.speaker: US government records
a1091.speech: According to US government records, in 2021 the Western power channelled about R2.6 billion ($148 million) for development assistance in Mali, with an additional R1.3 billion directed to humanitarian assistance.

a1091.speaker: Human Rights Watch (HRW)
a1091.speech: Says civilians are facing violence from the army and jihadists ; said it had telephonically interviewed 40 people with knowledge of the incidents in central Mali, the interviews conducted between March and May this year.

a1091.speaker: Carine Kaneza Nantulya, deputy director for Africa at Human Rights Watch (HRW)
a1091.speech: Said regional bodies should pressure Mali to bring back the rule of law and protect civilians from arbitrary killings ; "The African Union and the Economic Community of West African States should express their concerns about grave abuses by the Malian armed forces and apparent allied Wagner Group fighters, and increase pressure on the Malian authorities to end these violations and hold those responsible to account."

a1091.speaker: 28-year-old man interviewed by HRW (anonymous)
a1091.speech: "I was at the market when the shooting started [and] I saw three military helicopters flying low, one of them firing."

a1091.speaker: Another interviewee of HRW in central Mali (anonymous)
a1091.speech: "Soldiers consider us as jihadists [Islamic fighters], but jihadists threatened to impose an embargo on our village if we didn't comply with their laws. State authorities are not here to protect us. We had no other choice but to accept their orders. And, now, soldiers treat us as terrorists. We are between a rock and a hard place."

a1126.speaker: U.S. officials and aid workers
a1126.speech: Say President Donald Trump's sweeping freeze on U.S. foreign assistance has threatened programs intended to counter al-Shabab bombmakers, contain the spread of al-Qaeda across West Africa and secure Islamic State prisoners in the Middle East ; U.S. officials say now-suspended programs across Africa were designed specifically to respond to national security threats and contain the spread of terrorism.

a1126.speaker: Donald Trump, U.S. President (executive order)
a1126.speech: Signed an executive order that said the "foreign aid industry and bureaucracy are not aligned with American interests" and "serve to destabilize world peace."

a1126.speaker: Four current and former U.S. officials (anonymous)
a1126.speech: Said that many of the affected programs were specifically designed to respond to national security threats, and that their suspension could endanger America and its international allies.

a1126.speaker: Former U.S. security official (anonymous)
a1126.speech: "This is not 'The Apprentice.' You can't just tell your partners: you're fired. Everything we give them from training and equipment to general advice is, by definition, foreign assistance, most of which they have come to depend on to sustain operations that WE have imposed to 'keep America safe!'"

a1126.speaker: U.S. defense official (anonymous)
a1126.speech: Said the sudden shutdown triggered security risks for some of the hundreds of American troops stationed in Somalia; contractors responsible for building and maintaining bases for U.S.-trained Somali special forces, known as Danab, left so abruptly that U.S. soldiers had to scramble to pick up the slack, and nearly 400 Danab graduates were left outside an American military base with no provision for food, fuel or electricity ; Said another private contractor, which conducts medevacs for wounded Somali soldiers, had personnel in a remote combat zone when the stop-work order came down, and it was unclear if they would be reimbursed for the return flight or any subsequent medevacs.

a1126.speaker: Lt. Col. Mohamed Mohamud Ahmed, head of the police forensics team in the criminal investigation division
a1126.speech: Said the Mogadishu lab provided fingerprints and other crime scene data to Interpol and the FBI. Last year, the lab worked on about 120 terrorist cases, "but all the activity has collapsed within one month. Our mentors have left, our IT licenses have expired."

a1126.speaker: Security expert who has worked extensively in Somalia (anonymous)
a1126.speech: "If all U.S. money stops forever, this war [against al-Shabab] is over very fast."

a1126.speaker: U.N. panel of experts who study the Islamic State and al-Qaeda (report)
a1126.speech: A report this month said the threat posed by the groups "remained undiminished," and that both continued to shift their focus to Africa. The report also noted that al-Shabab was developing a "transactional or opportunistic" relationship with the Houthis in Yemen, whose fighters have targeted global shipping lanes.

a1126.speaker: Former U.S. security official (anonymous)
a1126.speech: Said U.S. support helps Kenyan police secure the porous, 430-mile border with Somalia, counter the threat of improvised explosive devices (IEDs) — which have killed hundreds of security forces and civilians — and respond to terrorist attacks; he pointed to one critical border program, now suspended, that uses U.S.-provided drones for surveillance, detection and interdiction of militants.

a1126.speaker: Kenyan police report (reviewed by The Washington Post)
a1126.speech: The drones allowed Kenyan forces to discover caches of water in jerricans hidden in remote areas by al-Shabab; on another occasion, the report said, a patrol disrupted men trying to plant a bomb.

a1126.speaker: Sam Mattock, director of the Halliday Finch security company
a1126.speech: "U.S. and international involvement is a game changer as far as the local units are concerned."

a1126.speaker: Security expert who has worked extensively in Somalia (anonymous)
a1126.speech: "I agree with Trump and wish my government had the balls to stop the foreign aid and focus on our people. But why not give everyone 90 days to plead their cases on an individual basis and if they cannot, then stop the money?"

a1126.speaker: Senior U.S. military official (anonymous)
a1126.speech: Said a multiyear program to train the army for counterterrorism operations in Benin has been put on hold; said two four-year programs for U.S. contractors to train local troops in Ivory Coast have also been paused, both initiatives having just begun in January, one focused on casualty care and the other on pre-deployment training ; "When you take that away, our ability to shape the environment is gone. And if nature abhors a vacuum, we know that predator nations will dive in."

a1126.speaker: Aneliese Bernard, former State Department adviser who now runs Strategic Stabilization Advisors
a1126.speech: "It is the worst possible timing to pause. It is hugely disruptive to the government's ability to repel terrorist attacks."

a1126.speaker: Aid worker with knowledge of the situation (anonymous)
a1126.speech: Said the funding freeze led to a three-day stoppage in humanitarian aid to the al-Hol and Roj camps before temporary waivers were issued to organizations working there, and that the guards' waivers need to be renewed every two weeks to avoid further disruption while aid work across the rest of Syria remains paused ; "When people don't have the water, the food, the things that they are relying on, they're going to look for someplace else to find it. The concern, especially in Syria with [the Islamic State] looking for opportunities to regroup, is that they will step into that vacuum."

a1126.speaker: Evan Jabro, Iraq's migration and displacement minister
a1126.speech: According to her, the camp in southern Iraq where returnees from al-Hol were being sent for rehabilitation has ceased operations due to lack of funding.

a1126.speaker: Congressional aide familiar with discussions (anonymous)
a1126.speech: Said members of Congress are still in the dark about how the administration is granting exemptions: "We've not seen criteria for the waiver process … and the few publicized waivers are barely being implemented. We see no evidence of a review process." ; Said the State Department has said it is terminating $1 billion worth of programs, but Congress has "no way to assess the legal, financial, or national security risks."

a1139.speaker: Volodymyr Zelenskyy, President of Ukraine
a1139.speech: Sharply raised his demand for air defence systems, saying on Tuesday that Ukraine needed a dozen additional Patriot systems to insulate its economy from the war. In April Zelenskyy had said Ukraine needed a minimum of seven Patriot systems to provide air cover.

a1139.speaker: Volodymyr Zelenskyy, President of Ukraine
a1139.speech: Said that last week Russia used almost 500 glide bombs, whose warhead ranges from 250kg (550lbs) to three tonnes, more than 400 strike drones, and almost 20 missiles of various types against Ukraine's front lines and civilian infrastructure.

a1139.speaker: Donald Trump, US President-elect
a1139.speech: Told NBC in an interview that he was open to reducing military aid to Ukraine and pulling the US out of NATO. "Possibly," he said, when asked if Kyiv should prepare for less aid from the US.

a1139.speaker: Donald Trump, US President-elect
a1139.speech: Has previously pledged to end the Ukraine war quickly, but unlike US President Biden has not upheld Ukraine's territorial integrity as a priority.

a1149.speaker: Alfonso Chikuni, Principal Secretary for Energy of Malawi
a1149.speech: Said President Lazarus Chakwera is expected to sign the compact at an event in Tanzania in January next year under a joint initiative called Project 300 by the World Bank and Africa Development Bank (AfDB). "We have lined up a number of projects. For instance, we are developing a compact, similar to the one that was done under the Millennium Challenge Account but this one will be financed by the World Bank and AfDB. So far, about $500 million has been pledged and President Lazarus Chakwera is going to sign the compact, alongside other 10 African heads of State, in Tanzania in January. So, we are moving very quickly."

a1149.speaker: Alfonso Chikuni, Principal Secretary for Energy of Malawi
a1149.speech: Said other key infrastructure projects are the eastern and western power backbone power lines that will ensure Malawi is internally and regionally connected.

a1149.speaker: World Bank brief about the Project 300 initiative
a1149.speech: Project 300 will see the World Bank, through International Development Association (IDA), spending $30 billion through concessional lending.

a1240.speaker: Presidency Communications, Ghana (statement signed by Felix Kwakye Ofosu, Spokesperson to the President)
a1240.speech: “President John Dramani Mahama has directed the Minister for Finance, Hon Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, to take urgent steps to bridge the funding gap arising out of the suspension of the USAID's international funding programme.” ; “Of particular concern to the President, is the impact of the projected $78.2 million shortfall that will adversely impact such critical interventions as malaria prevention, maternal and child health, family planning, reproductive health, nutrition and the fight against HIV/AIDS under which the availability of antiretroviral drugs, testing, and prevention programs are threatened.” ; The President expressed deep concern over the funding gap estimated at $156 million and has requested that the bridging arrangements focus on these priority areas to mitigate any deleterious effects occasioned by the USAID funding disruptions.

a1240.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a1240.speech: Has long advocated for aligning foreign aid with his “America First” policy ; posted on Truth Social, stating that USAID’s spending “IS TOTALLY UNEXPLAINABLE... CLOSE IT DOWN!” ; has consistently criticized foreign aid, arguing that it is an inefficient use of taxpayer money, and has been particularly vocal about USAID, highlighting specific expenditures he deems wasteful.

a1240.speaker: Elon Musk, tech billionaire collaborating with the White House
a1240.speech: Has previously called USAID “a criminal organization” and claimed Trump had agreed to dismantle it ; promoted a debunked claim that the agency funded Hollywood celebrities’ visits to Ukraine.

a1240.speaker: The White House
a1240.speech: Has listed several projects as examples of “waste and abuse,” including a $1.5 million grant to an LGBTQ group in Serbia, $2.5 million for electric vehicles in Vietnam, and $6 million for tourism in Egypt.

a1280.speaker: Small Scale Farmers Development Agency (SAFADA)
a1280.speech: has warned that Zambians should brace themselves for hard times as the new dawn government has failed to manage the agriculture sector.

a1280.speaker: Boyd Moobwe, SAFADA chief executive officer
a1280.speech: has cited policy inconsistency in the agriculture sector as some of the major failures of the UPND government, which he says had resulted in the sector failing to perform. He said the new dawn Government had messed up the agriculture sector which was worrying.

a1280.speaker: Boyd Moobwe, SAFADA chief executive officer
a1280.speech: said the assurances by President Hakainde Hichilema that things will change especially with measures put in place to stabilize the agriculture sector was not attainable because the cost of production had remained high. He said the cost of production had remained high, therefore, Zambians would see further upward price adjustment of commodities; he predicts harder times for Zambians as prices of basic commodities continue to escalate.

a1280.speaker: Boyd Moobwe, SAFADA chief executive officer
a1280.speech: said the cancellation of the fertiliser tender would result in late farming input distribution and this would cost the yield for the next harvesting season.

a1280.speaker: Boyd Moobwe, SAFADA chief executive officer
a1280.speech: said it was shocking that exportation of mealie meal had continued whilst the country was experiencing a shortage of the commodity.

a1408.speaker: Uchizi Mkandawire, Minister of Youths and Sports of Malawi
a1408.speech: On Thursday asked over 1000 Technical Entrepreneurial and Vocational Education (TEVETA) graduates from Mangochi and Zomba to embrace entrepreneurship in order to create employment for their fellow youths ; said the graduates can reduce unemployment level in the country especially if they start opening up their small scale businesses there by creating self-employment as well as employment for others ; said it is President Dr Lazarus Chakwera's version to see that many youths are equipped with technical skills and open up their businesses soon after graduation ; said there is a room for those without or with small business capital to obtain a loan from National Economic Empowerment Fund (NEEF) that President Chakwera initiated.

a1408.speaker: Uchizi Mkandawire, Minister of Youths and Sports of Malawi
a1408.speech: Thanked the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) for its financial support of the whole initiative through Titukulane Project: "As government, we want to thank USAID through its Titukulane Project for the initiative because it helped to equip the Youths with different technical skills. And to the graduates, please go and embrace entrepreneurship."

a1408.speaker: Elwin Sichiola, TEVETA executive director
a1408.speech: In his remarks, while thanking USAID, said the country needs to have more programs like Titukulane Project.

a1453.speaker: Erica Carr, USAID acting executive director (internal email)
a1453.speech: Ordered the mass destruction of sensitive documents stored at the agency's former headquarters; the directive, sent by email, mentions the destruction of "classified safes and personnel documents," asked employees to gather for a full day of document destruction at the Ronald Reagan Building, and recommended using shredders as a priority, reserving burn bags for cases where shredders were not available.

a1453.speaker: Politico
a1453.speech: Obtained the internal email asking employees to gather for a full day of document destruction at the Ronald Reagan Building.

a1453.speaker: The Washington Post
a1453.speech: Reports that the targeted documents included classified files and information on the agency's personnel.

a1453.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a1453.speech: According to him, more than 80% of USAID's programmes have been cancelled and the majority of employees have been dismissed or placed on administrative leave.

a1453.speaker: Legal experts and former employees cited by NBC and The Washington Post
a1453.speech: Point out that this directive could contravene the Federal Records Act of 1950, which requires the preservation of government records; some are concerned about a possible attempt to erase evidence linked to the agency's contested restructuring.

a1453.speaker: Elon Musk, head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)
a1453.speech: Reacted strongly on X, stating that "destroying evidence is a crime" ; Musk and Donald Trump have repeatedly criticised USAID, describing it as a "criminal organisation" accused of mismanaging public funds.

a1453.speaker: Gregory Meeks, US Representative (cited by The Washington Post)
a1453.speech: Denounced a possible attempt to conceal irregularities, at a time when several legal challenges are contesting the dismantling of the agency.

a1453.speaker: Anna Kelly, second spokesperson for the US presidency (White House)
a1453.speech: Said on social media that the documents destroyed were "old" and that "the originals still exist on classified computer systems."

a1565.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a1565.speech: According to the IMF, China's economy is expected to rebound by 8.1pc this year.

a1565.speaker: United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD)
a1565.speech: The trade, investment and development wing of the United Nations revised US GDP growth up to 4.7pc.

a1565.speaker: Organisation for Economic Cooperation & Development (OECD)
a1565.speech: Was even more bullish, revising its previous estimates in December by over a percentage point to 5.6pc, owing mainly to vaccine rollouts and the US stimulus.

a1565.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia
a1565.speech: In an Op-Ed piece, the Prime Minister has argued for debt relief and an increase in the issuance of special drawing rights (SDRs).

a1565.speaker: United States government
a1565.speech: The largest bilateral contributor of humanitarian aid at close to one billion dollars annually, the United States has raised concerns over what it considers an act of ethnic cleansing in the north.

a1565.speaker: President of the European Union
a1565.speech: Has stressed that all foreign policy tools are on the table, after the EU suspended budget support amounting to 107 million dollars last December.

a1679.speaker: A middle-aged woman in Tigray Regional State (unnamed)
a1679.speech: She shared her plight with a journalist: her empty home and markets beyond the reach of her impoverished means.

a1679.speaker: Another woman in Tigray Regional State (unnamed)
a1679.speech: Recounts a tale steeped in loss - the death of her sister to famine, a tragedy that leaves behind orphans and a community haplessly trying to overcome the relentless grip of hunger.

a1679.speaker: Tigray regional authorities
a1679.speech: Disclosed that two million people in Tigray are facing starvation.

a1679.speaker: United Nations (recent humanitarian estimate)
a1679.speech: Uncovered the magnitude of the crisis: to feed a third of those in need, a daunting 2.9 billion dollars is required in 2024.

a1679.speaker: UNICEF (report)
a1679.speech: Disclosed that up to 1.8 million children with disabilities are in dire need of immediate aid.

a1679.speaker: Amartya Sen, Nobel laureate in economics (1981 thesis)
a1679.speech: Argued that famine is less about food scarcity and more about economic, social, and political structures that fail to ensure equal access to food. His research, informed by studies of famines in Bengal (1940s) and Ethiopia (1970s), brought to light that famine results from inequitable economic structures, policy misjudgments, and social disparities. ; Sen's advocacy for inclusive economic growth and equitable distribution urged the need for policies beyond increasing food production to ensuring that growth benefits all segments of society.

a1679.speaker: Major donors USAID and the World Food Program (WFP)
a1679.speech: Have blamed mismanagement and theft in suspending aid, harming the victims instead.

a1679.speaker: Ethiopian federal government
a1679.speech: Its acknowledgement of the crisis in 2015 was a step in the right direction, but current conditions demand more than recognition.

a1735.speaker: South Korea's Personal Information Protection Commission (personal data protection watchdog)
a1735.speech: Said South Korea has banned new downloads of China's DeepSeek artificial intelligence chatbot ; said the AI model will become available again to South Korean users when "improvements and remedies" are made to ensure it complies with the country's personal data protection laws ; said the DeepSeek app became unavailable on Apple's App Store and Google Play on Saturday evening.

a1735.speaker: Choi Sang-mok, South Korea's acting president
a1735.speech: has described Deepseek as a "shock", that could impact the country's industries, beyond AI.

a1735.speaker: Lawmakers in the US
a1735.speech: have proposed a bill banning DeepSeek from federal devices, citing surveillance concerns.

a1856.speaker: Amina Mohammed, UN Deputy Secretary-General
a1856.speech: Said on Wednesday that more than 70 heads of state and government would attend.

a1856.speaker: Sources (anonymous)
a1856.speech: Said the event could be more successful without U.S. attendees trying to water down objectives, and that there is a strong consensus that the world must take urgent action on issues such as climate adaptation funding.

a1856.speaker: United Nations (estimate)
a1856.speech: The U.N. pegs the global financing gap for sustainable development at a whopping $4 trillion.

a1856.speaker: Seville Commitment (38-page negotiated document)
a1856.speech: Focuses on reforms to help poor nations adapt to climate crises, such as debt swaps, natural disasters debt pause clauses and an exploration of "global solidarity levies", which could tax highly polluting activities - or the super-rich - to finance sustainable development; it also targets progress towards better debt restructuring frameworks and innovations to boost funding, such as multilateral development banks' efforts to leverage special drawing rights.

a2070.speaker: Trump administration
a2070.speech: Has put the brakes on foreign aid while alleging it's wasteful.

a2070.speaker: United Nations AIDS agency (UNAIDS)
a2070.speech: "In the next five years, we could have 6.3 million AIDS-related deaths," the agency told The Associated Press.

a2070.speaker: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
a2070.speech: "Without HIV treatment, people with AIDS typically survive about three years."

a2070.speaker: US National Institutes of Health (NIH)
a2070.speech: Says opportunistic diseases include fungal infections, pneumonia, salmonella and tuberculosis.

a2070.speaker: Health experts
a2070.speech: Say that restoring the effects caused by the Trump administration's foreign aid freeze during a 90-day review period, and understanding what's allowed under the waiver for PEPFAR, will take time that many people don't have.

a2074.speaker: Julio Saramala and Moises Nhanombe, economists
a2074.speech: Warn of the need for structural reforms to ensure the sustainability of the Economic and Social Plan and State Budget (PESOE) 2026; both consider that, although the Government has proposed an increase of 22.8 billion meticais in the budget, the expansion of public spending faces limitations due to insufficient revenue collection, moderate economic growth and persistent inflation ; according to the specialists, formalising the informal sector is crucial to broadening the tax base, increasing State revenue and reducing dependence on external financing, and both agree that a large part of the budget continues to be channelled to operating expenses, limiting investment in education, health and infrastructure.

a2074.speaker: Mozambican Government
a2074.speech: Proposes for next year a general budget of 535.6 billion meticais, an increase of 22.8 billion relative to the 2025 budget, with about 70% allocated to State operating expenses.

a2074.speaker: Julio Saramala, economist
a2074.speech: Considers that the challenge lies not only in the numbers but in the State's capacity to collect revenue and apply resources efficiently: "More than expanding the budget, the Government must assess its execution capacity and the real need for the new expenditures foreseen" ; said Mozambique essentially has two options to finance the budget deficit, raising taxes or resorting to public debt, both with negative impacts; explained that raising taxes reduces households' purchasing power and limits private investment, while public debt "ends up competing with the private sector," an effect known as crowding out; stressed that the problem is not a lack of productive capacity but the country's difficulty in retaining wealth internally because of tax exemptions, capital flight and business conducted outside the country.

a2074.speaker: Julio Saramala, economist
a2074.speech: Argues that formalising the informal sector, which represents more than 50% of the economy and employs about 80% of the population, is essential to guaranteeing a full-employment economy and increasing revenue collection without raising taxes, and also advocates a deep budgetary reform eliminating waste and clarifying priorities so that resources saved are applied to productive sectors.

a2074.speaker: Moises Nhanombe, economist
a2074.speech: Warns of fiscal risks and the need for reforms in PESOE 2026, considering that low economic growth, dependence on a few sectors for revenue generation and high external public debt increase the State's vulnerability to exchange-rate fluctuations and international interest rates; stresses that increasing domestic production is crucial to reducing external dependence ; advocates a broad fiscal reform including broadening the tax base, formalising the informal sector and rationalising public spending: "Cuts and the redistribution of resources must prioritise sectors with greater immediate social impact, ensuring efficiency and transparency in budget execution"; adds that diversifying financing sources and developing public-private partnerships are essential, and that these measures will allow Mozambique to depend less on foreign aid.

a2074.speaker: Moises Nhanombe and Julio Saramala, economists
a2074.speech: Reacting to the inconsistencies in the 2024 General State Account, argue for the need for greater transparency, monitoring and auditing in the budget process as a way of guaranteeing the effectiveness of public policies and international confidence; both stress that without rigorous oversight it is difficult to ensure that State resources are applied efficiently, and that the budget must follow an integrated cycle of forecasting, execution and monitoring with timely audits.

a2074.speaker: Moises Nhanombe, economist
a2074.speech: Stressed that "in various budget documents, we have seen discrepancies between what was forecast and what was monitored, between declared expenditures and those that are actually carried out," saying these inconsistencies highlight transparency problems in the Government ; "When public spending is not transparent, audited or monitored, it ends up greatly affecting its execution and, above all, prioritisation."

a2074.speaker: Julio Saramala, economist
a2074.speech: Highlighted the importance of effective audits and rigorous budget execution: "The executor of the State is the Ministry of Finance, and the auditor is the Administrative Tribunal. That is how it should be. Depending on each source of financing, some external auditor may come in and an independent audit commission may even be created" ; warned that implementation of projects does not always follow what was planned, recalling that out of 138 indicators foreseen for 2025 fewer than 50% were actually executed: "When we look at the State budget, we should ask: if some projects are not implemented in full, who audits the corresponding amounts? It is the Administrative Tribunal. But, unfortunately, the timings are not always ideal."

a2074.speaker: Julio Saramala, economist
a2074.speech: Stressed the importance of maintaining international confidence, essential for the country's external financing: "After blockages from the IMF, we recently had the visit of the CEO of the World Bank, as well as that of the Millennium Challenge Corporation. It is crucial that this confidence remains stable to guarantee a bigger oxygen balloon for the country."

a2074.speaker: Julio Saramala, economist
a2074.speech: Warned of the risks of poor execution in the current economic context: "We are going through an economic recession, due to various factors, including post-electoral tension. Without planned and audited budget execution, there is a risk of the recession worsening, unemployment rising, high inflation and macroeconomic imbalances. There is still much to do to ensure that the budget is implemented efficiently and that the country returns to sustainable economic growth."

a2211.speaker: The Catholic Church in Malawi
a2211.speech: Has publicly condemned Chakwera's government for financial mismanagement, failed economic policies, and an impending hunger crisis - especially in the wake of Cyclone Freddy, where state relief efforts fell woefully short.

a2211.speaker: Afrobarometer survey
a2211.speech: Recent Afrobarometer survey results show 76% of Malawians believe the country is heading in the wrong direction; if elections were held today, 43% of respondents would vote for Mutharika's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), compared to 29% for the ruling Malawi Congress Party (MCP); 84% of Malawians say they will "definitely" vote in the upcoming election.

a2211.speaker: Joseph de Maistre, philosopher
a2211.speech: "Every nation gets the government it deserves."

a2211.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a2211.speech: Came to power in 2020 promising to create a thriving economy and tackle youth unemployment, including an ambitious pledge to generate one million jobs.

a2224.speaker: Numene Bartekwa, Grand Kru County Senator (Liberia)
a2224.speech: Wants the Liberian Government to prioritize the construction of Southeastern roads amid international support, and named the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) Fund, IMF Credit Facility Fund, and the World Bank's contribution as some of the international supports: "Road connectivity is key in the development of any nation, and as such, prioritizing the Southeastern roads will be a milestone."

a2224.speaker: Numene Bartekwa, Grand Kru County Senator (Liberia)
a2224.speech: Added that the people of Grand Kru County and other counties in the South East have suffered a lot due to the lack of a good road network, and called on the government to ensure that the roads are paved to boost economic development across the country.

a2367.speaker: Nigeria Auto Manufacturers Association (NAMA)
a2367.speech: Has disclosed that Nigeria imports 1m vehicles annually, and that out of the 1m vehicles, only about 14,000 representing 1.4 per cent are brand new.

a2367.speaker: Dr. Harpreet Singh, Representative of the Nigeria Auto Manufacturers Association (NAMA)
a2367.speech: Regretted that while Nigeria had the capacity to develop its automotive industry given the huge market, the country is lagging behind due to absence of policy. He said: "We don't need to reinvent the wheel; we have an overload of capacity in this country. What is required is policy. We import a million units per year, not up to 14,000 of them are brand new vehicles. Lesser are made in Nigeria. We have the potential to create jobs for our youths. It pains me. Because there is no job, they go into other activities. If we create jobs in the North, we give them a sense of progress."

a2367.speaker: Dr. Harpreet Singh, Representative of the Nigeria Auto Manufacturers Association (NAMA)
a2367.speech: Assured that automotive manufacturers would continue to advocate backward integration. He said, "NAMA stands for backward integration, from fully assembled vehicles to manufacturing, built in Nigeria and made in Nigeria. Today we are the backbone of defence logistics. 400 trucks churned out in a month. We are supplying defence. In NAMA, our belief is backward integration and we strive to continue to do that. We bring all the automotive assemblers and manufacturers together. It is something that has to be done and has to be done right now. Nigeria is future ready for the automobile revolution."

a2367.speaker: Joseph Osanipin, Director-General of the National Automotive Design and Development Council (NADDC), represented by Deputy Director Felicia Oyebolu
a2367.speech: Called for a unified push towards the development of local content in Nigeria's automotive sector; tasked stakeholders to take advantage of the First Nigeria policy to create jobs, enhance value retention and reduce capital flight; identified local content development as the engine that would drive a transformative shift in Nigeria's automotive landscape and emphasised its importance in five key areas - economic diversification and job creation, capital retention, technology transfer, supply chain resilience, and improved product innovation. He said: "We must collectively address these challenges. Let us invest in local capabilities, champion innovation, and advocate for supportive policies."

a2367.speaker: African Association of Automotive Manufacturers (AAAM)
a2367.speech: In its contribution, stressed the need for Nigeria to legalize its automotive policy to provide the foundation for sustainable local manufacturing, job creation and boost investor's confidence.

a2367.speaker: Victoria Backhaus-Jerling, Chief Executive Officer, African Association of Automotive Manufacturers (AAAM)
a2367.speech: In her virtual presentation at the summit, maintained that without it, the sector would remain vulnerable to unchecked used imports, while the country also risked missing out on the opportunities industrialisation could provide.

a2388.speaker: Shivute, Commissioner of the Namibia Revenue Agency (NamRA)
a2388.speech: Expressed confidence in the agency’s ability to exceed its projected revenue target, speaking to Namibian Sun in Windhoek during the release of the Time Release Study report for the Trans-Kalahari Border Post: “By the end of March, we will not only meet but surpass the revenue target,” he said ; “In figures, we have collected N$83.1 billion. I am 100% confident that by March 2025, we will have exceeded our revenue target,” he added ; said that since its establishment NamRA has prioritised enhancing revenue collection while minimising financial leakage, and emphasised the agency’s role in ensuring that government funding remains stable: “We are building a cohesive team to ensure that whatever target the minister of finance assigns us, we put our heads, hearts and hands together to achieve it. This guarantees that the minister does not face difficulties in funding Namibia’s developmental agenda,” he noted.

a2388.speaker: Shivute, Commissioner of the Namibia Revenue Agency (NamRA)
a2388.speech: Highlighted Namibia’s progress in improving trade facilitation and border management and announced the finalisation of the national strategy for border management: “Today is a historic day as we have successfully completed the coordinated border management national strategy for Namibia. According to the World Trade Organisation’s trade facilitation agreement, member states must implement measures to reduce bureaucracy and enhance efficiency at borders,” he explained ; “We must work in a coordinated manner. Improving efficiency at our borders will attract more foreign direct investment. Many landlocked SADC countries rely on our ports, and by enhancing trade facilitation, we will boost economic growth, create jobs and drive Namibia towards prosperity,” Shivute said.

a2388.speaker: Sikongo Haihambo, executive director, Namibian ministry of trade and industrialisation
a2388.speech: Expressed disappointment over the absence of key stakeholders: “I must record my disappointment that a significant number of the 12 or 13 agencies involved in border operations are not present today,” he said ; compared the situation to a football team selection: “If you have not been practising, you will not be picked to play on Saturday or Sunday. Those who fail to engage may become a burden to others” ; urged absent agencies to participate actively, warning that inefficiencies at border posts could hinder trade and slow economic progress: “Imagine losing 20 days waiting for cargo to arrive – that is a lot of wasted time. Today marks a crucial step in ensuring a smoother and more efficient trade process,” he emphasised.

a2442.speaker: Two witnesses in Goma
a2442.speech: Told Reuters on Monday that Congolese M23 rebels have entered the centre of the eastern city of Goma.

a2442.speaker: One of the witnesses
a2442.speech: Shared a brief video showing heavily armed men walking through the streets.

a2442.speaker: United Nations Security Council
a2442.speech: Demanded on Sunday that M23 rebel forces stop an ongoing offensive and advance toward Goma, and that “external forces” in the region immediately withdraw ; urged Rwanda and the DRC to return to talks to achieve peace and address issues related to the presence of Rwanda Defence Forces in the eastern Congo and Congolese support for the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR).

a2442.speaker: M23 (Rwandan-backed rebel group)
a2442.speech: Said they had taken Goma following a lightning advance.

a2442.speaker: M23 (Rwandan-backed rebel group)
a2442.speech: Vows to defend Tutsi interests, particularly against ethnic Hutu militias such as the FDLR.

a2442.speaker: United States, France and Britain (at the UN Security Council meeting)
a2442.speech: Condemned what they said was Rwanda's backing of the M23 rebel advance.

a2442.speaker: Dorothy Shea, Acting US Ambassador to the UN
a2442.speech: Specifically called out Rwanda for using GPS jamming and spoofing.

a2442.speaker: UN Security Council (statement)
a2442.speech: “condemned the ongoing flagrant disregard for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the DRC, including the unauthorised presence in the Eastern DRC of external forces” and demanded that they “withdraw immediately” ; “The members of the Security Council are also deeply alarmed by continued occurrences of GPS jamming and spoofing activities in support of M23 operations in North Kivu, which represent imminent risk to civil aviation safety and negatively impact the delivery of humanitarian assistance to populations in need.”

a2516.speaker: MCC (email notification to staff)
a2516.speech: According to MCC staff notified by email this week, 'there will soon be a significant reduction' in programmes and personnel, with almost all employees slated for administrative leave as early as May 5 leaving only the acting CEO in place to satisfy statutory requirements.

a2516.speaker: MCC employees
a2516.speech: warned that the workforce reduction plan would eliminate virtually all project management capacity within the agency.

a2516.speaker: Ntsokoane Matekane, Prime Minister of Lesotho
a2516.speech: during the Compact II launch hailed the compact's commencement as “a major boost for Lesotho's investment programme” and urged that “every dollar invested…be used for the benefit of Basotho.” ; He stressed at its launch that “the countdown for the five‑year implementation of this programme has begun and we cannot afford any delays.”

a2516.speaker: Dr Retšelisitsoe Matlanyane, Finance Minister of Lesotho
a2516.speech: during the same event underscored the compact's strategic importance at a time when Lesotho's economy “is at a critical point.”

a2516.speaker: UNAIDS (report)
a2516.speech: according to a report released by UNAIDS last month, significant cuts to United States funding for HIV programmes have triggered widespread disruptions, threatening the country's progress in combating the epidemic ; According to UNAIDS, approximately 28 percent of PEPFAR support has resumed, 32 percent is still paused, and 40 percent is terminated, with “804 (53.3 percent) of the 1,508 human resources for health supported through PEPFAR funding” now out of work.

a2580.speaker: Rodney Wallace Doeseb, interim coach of the Namibian under-20 women's national team (Young Gladiators)
a2580.speech: told the NFA media desk: "Technically, the girls are promising - and now, we just have to make sure we get the combinations and tactics right ahead of the first leg. Away from home will be interesting; it will be a different ball game for our team, and we need to have that mental strength to hold our own and strive for a result," ; "These girls are still in school and have not played much, especially at this level - and now, they get this chance. Both sides will surely come out to play and put on a show. We look forward to the two legs indeed."

a2689.speaker: Elon Musk, American billionaire and owner of X
a2689.speech: Has described US Agency for International Development (USAID) as a criminal organisation, saying it is time for the agency to die. Reacting to @AutismCapital’s post on X, Musk said, “USAID is a criminal organisation. Time for it to die.”

a2689.speaker: Elon Musk, American billionaire and owner of X (quoted by CNN)
a2689.speech: “With regards to the USAID stuff, I went over it with (the president) in detail and he agreed that we should shut it down.” Musk also reportedly said he checked with Trump “a few times” and Trump confirmed he wants to shut down the agency.

a2689.speaker: @AutismCapital, X user
a2689.speech: An X user @AutismCapital posted the information on his account on Sunday, saying, “The DOGE members threatened to physically call the police after being refused entry. They were trying to access the security and personnel files.” The X user added, “Federal officials are concerned that Trump is trying to fold USAID into the US State Department in an effort to cut government corruption and bloat. USAID employs approximately 10,000 people, excluding contractors, with 2/3 of them overseas. 60 USAID members were already put on leave last week after trying to circumvent President Trump’s executive order on stopping foreign aid.”

a2689.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a2689.speech: On Sunday evening, Trump while commenting on USAID, reportedly told reporters, “It’s been run by a bunch of radical lunatics, and we’re getting them out, and then we’ll make a decision” on its future.

a2689.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State (memo, reported by Al Jazeera)
a2689.speech: In an accompanying memo, newly confirmed Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, directed senior officials to “ensure that, to the maximum extent permitted by law, no new obligations shall be made for foreign assistance”.

a2689.speaker: Humanitarian organisations
a2689.speech: Have raised alarm at the directive, expressing fears that it could contribute to global instability and loss of life.

a2689.speaker: Abby Maxman, head of Oxfam America
a2689.speech: Was quoted as saying in a statement, “By suspending foreign development assistance, the Trump administration is threatening the lives and futures of communities in crisis, and abandoning the United States’ long-held bipartisan approach to foreign assistance which supports people based on need, regardless of politics.”

a2856.speaker: USAID (statement on its website)
a2856.speech: Announced on Sunday 24 February that it would lay off about 1,600 employees in the United States and place the majority of its staff on administrative leave: “USAID is beginning the implementation of a reduction in force that will affect approximately 1,600 USAID employees posted in the United States” ; stated that all other employees directly employed by USAID worldwide would be placed on administrative leave by 11:59 p.m. Sunday, except those responsible for “essential mission functions, core leadership and/or specially designated programmes” ; stated that it would inform on Sunday the “designated essential personnel” who are to remain in post, without specifying their number, and that it will finance the repatriation costs of its staff deployed abroad, assuring that employees will have access to diplomatic resources until their return to the United States.

a2856.speaker: Donald Trump, US President (executive order)
a2856.speech: Signed an executive order on 20 January, the day of his return to the White House, ordering a freeze on US foreign aid for 90 days, for the duration of a complete review.

a2856.speaker: Najat Vallaud-Belkacem, former French Minister of National Education, and Guillaume Gonin, teacher (op-ed in Le Monde)
a2856.speech: Pointed to the “disastrous” consequences of the dismantling of USAID: “Since 2000, the agency estimates that it has saved 11.7 million lives and prevented 2.1 billion cases of malaria. But, for Elon Musk, it is a ‘nest of vipers of radical Marxists who hate America’” ; pointed to the unbalanced power relationship between the billionaire and the Trump administration and to food, health and social programmes around the world, such as undernutrition in Sudan and children born with HIV in Haiti, Zambia or Mozambique ; “Or how a dantesque butterfly effect has turned a state scandal into an immediate global tragedy.”

a2856.speaker: Elon Musk, head of “government efficiency” in the Trump administration
a2856.speech: Called USAID a “nest of vipers of radical Marxists who hate America” (quoted in the Le Monde op-ed).

a2856.speaker: The American press
a2856.speech: Had asserted that USAID’s workforce would be reduced to almost nothing.

a2856.speaker: A federal judge (US)
a2856.speech: On Friday had suspended the decision to block certain measures of the Trump administration.

a2856.speaker: USAID employee unions
a2856.speech: Said the measures of the Trump administration were aimed at dismantling the agency.

a2856.speaker: A USAID employee (anonymous)
a2856.speech: “We are not treated like human beings.”

a2862.speaker: Mohamed El-Shennawy, spokesman for the Egyptian presidency
a2862.speech: Said that the Ukrainian and Egyptian heads of state exchanged views on the latest developments in the war

a2862.speaker: Abdel Fattah al-Sissi, President of Egypt
a2862.speech: Reaffirmed the need to reach a political and diplomatic settlement, stressing the importance of dialogue to put an end to a conflict that has lasted more than three years, and gave assurances of his country's full support for any peace initiative aimed at bringing a swift end to hostilities

a2862.speaker: Abdel Fattah al-Sissi, President of Egypt, and Volodymyr Zelensky, President of Ukraine
a2862.speech: Addressed the situation in the Middle East, calling for respect for the ceasefire between Israel and Iran and for the resumption of negotiations with a view to a lasting solution

a2862.speaker: Abdel Fattah al-Sissi, President of Egypt
a2862.speech: Presented Egypt's efforts in favour of a ceasefire in the Gaza Strip and to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid to civilians

a2939.speaker: U.S. Senator John "Jack" Reed and U.S. Representative Gabriel Felix Kofi Amo
a2939.speech: Have emphasized the importance of sustained investment in Liberia's Education Sector; made a firm commitment to advocate for continued support to the country's Education Sector during a one-day visit to the Ministry of Education to assess the impact of USAID's support on the country's educational development ; expressed their desire to learn as much as possible about the impacts of the recent cuts, while also hearing directly from local leaders about areas of progress.

a2939.speaker: Nyekpeh Forkpa, Deputy Education Minister for Administration of Liberia
a2939.speech: Thanked the U.S. government for its longstanding support to Liberia's Education Sector; highlighted the critical role USAID has played in strengthening Liberia's education system, particularly through teacher training programs and institutional capacity building. He said, "USAID's support enabled thousands of students to pursue education locally and abroad, while also helping to establish systems for data collection and analysis that inform national education policy". ; Noted that the recent adjustments to USAID programming have forced Liberia to make internal shifts, including reallocating resources and assuming direct responsibility for initiatives such as school feeding.

a2986.speaker: Macka Traoré, Commissioner General of the Fria Festival (Fristival)
a2986.speech: At the outset, the Commissioner General of Fristival explained the reason for the choice of Chef Galé. According to Macka Traoré, this choice is explained by the years of sacrifice and the instilling of the true values of scouting, but beyond that, of true values in the children of Fria. ; "We said to ourselves that instead of always paying tribute to people posthumously, it is better to pay tribute to them while they are still here, so that their families can be even prouder of them. Everyone agreed that Chef Galé should be honoured."

a2986.speaker: Macka Traoré, Commissioner General of the Fria Festival (Fristival)
a2986.speech: Returning to the 9th Fristival itself, the Commissioner General hammered home what makes this year special: "This year, Father Christmas will walk through Fria like when we were little. In every neighbourhood of Fria, we will give gifts to the children. We will bring that back to life. Because there are children of ten years ago who do not know that this used to happen here. The Feu de Caen, we started it last year. So we will continue the Feu de Caen this year. There are also the former Syli players who will play a gala match. We will put the schools in competition. The winners will get tablets and everything."

a2986.speaker: Macka Traoré, Commissioner General of the Fria Festival (Fristival)
a2986.speech: "This appointment of hope offers not only humanitarian aid but also an exceptional programme with artists such as Singleton, Fishkiller, Sheba Queen, Koury Simple and many others on stage. These artists, also present at this conference, each promised the best of themselves," Macka Traoré listed, in conclusion.

a3018.speaker: Owen Chataika, Mchinji District Health Office spokesperson
a3018.speech: Says the district is still registering new leprosy cases: “This year, already there are some new cases that have already been registered, which is something worrying” ; “The new cases show that leprosy is still a hidden problem in our communities.”

a3018.speaker: Owen Chataika, Mchinji District Health Office spokesperson
a3018.speech: “The district health office plans to decentralise leprosy clinics and lobby for more funds for mobile clinics, contact tracing and community sensitisation.”

a3018.speaker: Dickens Chimatiro, National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Elimination Programme monitoring and evaluation officer
a3018.speech: “It is a cause for us to worry because even though we reached the elimination level in 1994, there are still other districts that are reporting more than one leprosy case per 10 000 people” ; “Since 2024, we have registered 367 new cases.”

a3018.speaker: National Tuberculosis and Leprosy Elimination Programme
a3018.speech: According to the national programme, more than 600 people in the country are undergoing leprosy treatment.

a3018.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a3018.speech: According to the WHO, the disease is transmitted through prolonged and close contact with droplets from the nose and mouth of an untreated case, and does not spread through casual contact like shaking hands or hugging, sharing meals or sitting next to each other.

a3018.speaker: Maziko Matemba, community health commentator
a3018.speech: Says the new cases are food for thought for health authorities: “As a country, we should ask ourselves why there is a resurgence of the disease after about three decades” ; Says the country should confront what has gone wrong and learn from past strategies that helped eliminate the outbreak: “Factors contributing to the resurgence can be many, but they could include gaps in disease surveillance and prevention. When we say we have eliminated a disease, we also must have strong systems which control its recurrence. We have to check our systems to understand what has gone wrong, including financing for leprosy programmes.”

a3083.speaker: Tlokweng Parliamentary Office (statement)
a3083.speech: According to the statement, the session will bring together key figures from the constituency in a dynamic forum designed to foster dialogue and sharing of ideas on economic opportunities embedded in the national budget.

a3083.speaker: Phenyo Segokgo, Member of Parliament for Tlokweng
a3083.speech: Has emphasised the importance of simplifying the budget to encourage local engagement: “The planning committee has invited industry captains to break down the budget in an easily digestible way so that BaTlokwa can understand it,” he said in the statement.

a3083.speaker: Phenyo Segokgo, Member of Parliament for Tlokweng
a3083.speech: Linked the initiative to President Gideon Duma Boko’s broader vision for national transformation: “The President, in his maiden State of the Nation Address, declared that Botswana is embarking on a journey of renewal and restoration” ; “As a responsible MP, I heeded his clarion call and sought to restore trust and accountability with my constituents. We want BaTlokwa to understand the budget, own it, and explore opportunities through which they can revitalise the economy by empowering themselves.”

a3083.speaker: Gideon Duma Boko, President of Botswana
a3083.speech: In his maiden State of the Nation Address, declared that Botswana is embarking on a journey of renewal and restoration.

a3176.speaker: Mykyta Sukhorhova, 31-year-old dancer with the National Ballet of Ukraine from eastern Ukraine
a3176.speech: Said dancing was his way of supporting his country ; "I'm not in military... I can do what I can do" ; "If I can help in this, in this side of life, you know, it's really good."

a3220.speaker: Lesetja Kganyago, South African Reserve Bank Governor
a3220.speech: Said at a monetary policy committee briefing on Wednesday that South Africa is "at a difficult juncture" regarding food prices, and that hot and dry weather caused by El Nino may lead food inflation to pick up again ; "It looks like the risk to the crops could materialise more than what we thought of last year" ; said that, as we have seen in the past, that poses a risk to food inflation and complicates the disinflation process.

a3220.speaker: Lesetja Kganyago, South African Reserve Bank Governor
a3220.speech: Reaffirmed Wednesday after the MPC maintained its benchmark rate at a 15-year high of 8.25% for a fifth meeting in a row that it will only cut rates when it is confident that inflation is on a sustainable path toward the midpoint of its 3% to 6% target range, where it prefers to anchor expectations.

a3220.speaker: Bloomberg's Shisa Nyama Index (data/index)
a3220.speech: Shows the average price of a backyard braai rose 1.3% in March from a year earlier, compared with 2.5% in the prior month.

a3220.speaker: Government's Crop Estimates Committee
a3220.speech: Cut its outlook for the white corn harvest by 11% to 6.28 million tons on Tuesday, while the overall take that includes the yellow variety is projected at a five-year low of 13.3 million tons.

a3220.speaker: South African Reserve Bank (central bank models)
a3220.speech: The central bank's models show severe drought conditions could add 10 to 28 percentage points to food inflation.

a3220.speaker: Pietermaritzburg Economic Justice and Dignity group (PMBEJD) data
a3220.speech: The Shisa Nyama Index crunches data from the PMBEJD of 14 key ingredients in barbecues consumed in South African townships; to compile its survey, the PMBEJD's data collectors track food prices on the shelves of 47 supermarkets and 32 butcheries that target the low-income market in the greater areas of Johannesburg, Durban, Cape Town, Pietermaritzburg and Springbok.

a3246.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a3246.speech: Declared on Friday that the United States is halting all federal funding in favour of South Africa ; denounces in particular the "racial and discriminatory confiscation of land" ; announced on Friday, because of the "horrible" treatment imposed by the South African government, that access to American citizenship would be made easier for any South African farmer who wishes to emigrate to the United States.

a3246.speaker: U.S. presidential executive order halting aid to South Africa
a3246.speech: Asserts that white South Africans are being unjustly discriminated against and orders the end of foreign aid.

a3246.speaker: White House
a3246.speech: According to the White House, the "racial and discriminatory confiscation of land" is allowed by an expropriation law promulgated in January by South African President Cyril Ramaphosa.

a3246.speaker: U.S. government data
a3246.speech: American foreign aid commitments to South Africa amounted to 323.4 million dollars in 2024, according to U.S. government data.

a3260.speaker: Rilwanu Mohammed, Executive Chairman of the Bauchi State Primary Health Care Development Board
a3260.speech: Stated that the suspension of the activities of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) has impacted the distribution of family planning commodities, explaining that the suspension has led to challenges in ensuring a steady supply of family planning commodities to health facilities across the state ; Explained that USAID was responsible for the last-mile distribution of family planning commodities to primary healthcare facilities across the state: "However, with the suspension of their activities, these facilities are now facing stockouts, in spite of the increasing demand for family planning services at the community level" ; Revealed that the board was holding meetings to ensure that family planning commodities reached all health facilities and that there was no diversion of supplies ; Expressed regret over the suspension of USAID's activities, which resulted from a decision by US President Donald Trump, and emphasised the negative impact on family planning services in the state ; Mentioned that the Bauchi State government had allocated N50 million as counterpart funding for the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) to supply family planning commodities ; Commended the J4PD for its ongoing efforts in advocating for family planning, immunisation, and other maternal, newborn, and child health services.

a3260.speaker: Bashir Hassan, knowledge and communication specialist, Journalists for Public Health and Development Initiative (J4PD)
a3260.speech: Speaking on behalf of J4PD, assured that the organisation would continue to support the agency in raising public awareness, and emphasised that increasing the uptake of healthcare services would contribute to the state's economic development.

a3276.speaker: IATF2020 Advisory Council
a3276.speech: Endorsed the decision to postpone the second Intra-African Trade Fair by one year during its sixth meeting held virtually on 26 April 2020, after careful assessment of the situation; also decided to postpone the third edition of IATF from 2022 to 2023 to be in line with the two-year intervals between IATF events.

a3276.speaker: Prof. Benedict Oramah, Afreximbank President
a3276.speech: Said that the continuing COVID-19 pandemic situation was not conducive to holding such an important pan African event which was initially scheduled to take place in just 4 months: "The COVID-19 pandemic has forced Governments, corporations and individuals to take unprecedented measures to ensure public safety." ; "It is our responsibility to comply with these measures to protect our host country and ensure the health and safety of all delegates, exhibitors and participants who have confirmed or expressed interest in taking part in the second edition of IATF."

a3276.speaker: Johns Hopkins University
a3276.speech: Africa has more than 35 million coronavirus confirmed cases, 11,336 recovered and 1,524 deaths as at the end of April 29.

a3276.speaker: Amb. Albert Muchanga, Commissioner for Trade and Industry of the African Union
a3276.speech: Stressing the need to enable participants to fully benefit from the opportunities offered by the trade fair, said that the postponement would allow stakeholders to focus on the urgent collective task of responding to the pandemic: "We are facing an unprecedented health crisis. This is the time to join efforts to also mitigate the impact of the pandemic on African economies. We have agreed that the second IATF needed to take place in a more favourable context to enable African countries and companies to take full advantage of the Trade Fair, which will now become an element of their recovery strategy."

a3276.speaker: Soraya Hakuziyaremye, Minister of Trade and Industry of Rwanda
a3276.speech: Reiterated the commitment of the government of Rwanda to the success of the trade fair: "The reality we are confronted with today as we fight the spread of Covid-19 has prompted us to look at various factors which will undoubtedly impact African businesses and investors this year. In partnership with Afreximbank and the AU Commission, Rwanda is looking forward to the second IATF in 2021 to boost intra African trade, which is more than ever crucial to the development of our continent."

a3276.speaker: Chief Olusegun Obasanjo, IATF Advisory Council Chairman and former President of Nigeria
a3276.speech: "We offer sincere condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of all those who have lost their lives because of the coronavirus. We also wish all those who have been affected by the virus speedy recovery. We hope that this pandemic will soon be overcome to enable normal businesses to resume and underpin the forthcoming Trade Fair."

a3409.speaker: Lisa Johnson, US Ambassador to Namibia
a3409.speech: Said at the launch of the first export of charcoal from Namibia directly to the US market that the exportation signals the commencement of a trade opportunity that could see Namibia export several thousand tons of premium grade charcoal to the US tariff-free each month; stated that the Namibian charcoal sector is a priority sector for export growth given the high rates of employment, the positive impact it has on the environment as well as the high growth potential ; "The US government will continue to support the Namibian private sector to prepare exporters to meet complex market entry requirements, including the need for certification, market-entry compliance, understanding buyer requirements, and linking Namibian exporters to US buyers."

a3409.speaker: Verna Sinimbo, Deputy Minister of Industrialisation and Trade of Namibia
a3409.speech: Said this export and subsequent exports will lead to socio-economic improvement of communities where it is needed most, especially as the Covid-19 pandemic continues to adversely affect the outlook for most global economies of which Namibia is no exception ; "The government regards charcoal as a major opportunity for both environmental sustainability and employment creation, especially in rural settings. Our 'black gold', charcoal is frontloaded by the ministry to ensure that Namibia accrues maximum benefit out of it."

a3409.speaker: Verna Sinimbo, Deputy Minister of Industrialisation and Trade of Namibia
a3409.speech: Noted that the ministry launched the construction of a factory to produce a variety of nutritional animal feed and biochar from Namibia's vast invader bush asset, located a few kilometres north of Otjiwarongo and set to open in 2022, which she said shows the ministry's efforts in promoting Namibia's charcoal industry; added that the ministry started in October 2020 to train SMEs in the charcoal sector's value chains, with around 30 SMEs trained so far and an aim of training at least 100 SMEs, particularly the youth and women.

a3421.speaker: Pele's daughter (social media post)
a3421.speech: Posted a photo of the Brazilian football legend from his hospital bed in Sao Paulo on Friday, December 23, 2022, with the caption "one more night together."

a3421.speaker: Abeka Ankrah, Hearts of Oak legend and former Ghana national team player
a3421.speech: Recalled the build-up to the 1969 match against Santos: "A week before we played the game, we were told we were going to face Santos. The Brazilian club was on a training tour. At that time, I was a national team player and had just returned from Niger after a match. I came back ill, but after taking some tablets, I felt fine. I had read a lot about Pele in the newspapers, so it felt great to play against him. I had to give my best to show the world that I had something to offer." ; "Santos liked to keep the ball."

a3421.speaker: Abeka Ankrah, Hearts of Oak legend and former Ghana national team player
a3421.speech: Described his goal: "A few minutes before the goal, I received the ball from our half, ran through the center, and shot. It was my trademark move, and it went into the net. It felt great. When I scored, the Santos goalkeeper even clapped in astonishment, and that made me even prouder."

a3421.speaker: Abeka Ankrah, Hearts of Oak legend and former Ghana national team player
a3421.speech: Described Pele as the greatest player he ever saw: "He was amazing - his positioning, his passing, his ability to cross the ball. He wasn't one to overcomplicate things. Pele showed us that it wasn't necessary to dribble past 10 or 15 players to make an impact." ; "His shooting and heading were a menace. And on no occasion did he make a bad pass." ; "Pele didn't dribble often, but when he did, it was clear that he was an intelligent player. He passed a lot and moved quickly. He shot frequently."

a3421.speaker: Abeka Ankrah, Hearts of Oak legend and former Ghana national team player
a3421.speech: Noted of Amusa Gbadamoshie: "Amusa was an excellent player. He exchanged pennants with Pele. While Pele was demonstrating for Santos, Amusa was doing his part for Hearts of Oak. The fans were the true judges."

a3421.speaker: Abeka Ankrah, Hearts of Oak legend and former Ghana national team player
a3421.speech: Explained Pele's lasting influence on Ghanaian football: "Any player who performed well, especially as a number 10, was called 'Pele.' Back then, if you played well, they would nickname you after Pele. He was known for his excellent positioning, and that's something we learned from him."

a3421.speaker: The newspapers (contemporary Ghanaian press reports)
a3421.speech: "It was a man-of-the-match-worthy performance," the newspapers said of Santos left winger Edu; the papers also said that with a few decisions going their way, Hearts could have achieved a surprising victory.

a3603.speaker: Dr. Marial Dongrin, Minister of Finance and Planning of South Sudan
a3603.speech: Speaking at the inauguration on Tuesday, said the institute is a key step in the government’s plan to professionalize the revenue system. “South Sudan Institute for Revenue Administration is more than a physical institution we are seeing today. It represents our resolve to professionalize and modernize our revenue system,” he said. ; “Through this institute we will have competent and ethical tax and custom professionals who will manage public resources transparently”, he added. ; “In training our officers, they will have not only the technical competence, but they will also have the leadership and managerial capabilities to manage our tax administration,” he said. The minister added that SSIRA graduates will be trained not just in technical knowledge, but also in leadership to support reforms in the country’s public finance system.

a3603.speaker: Dr. Marial Dongrin, Minister of Finance and Planning of South Sudan
a3603.speech: said while many African economies rely on tax revenue, South Sudan still depends largely on oil income, which he described as a risk to economic stability. He pointed to the country’s recent financial struggles caused by disruptions in oil production and export.

a3661.speaker: Note/communique received by APA (African Union)
a3661.speech: Underlines that, through a grant of $200,000, the African Union joins by this act of solidarity a growing international mobilization in favor of Liberia ; states that the donation, intended to respond to the urgent needs of the affected communities, testifies to the AU's commitment to humanitarian aid and African solidarity.

a3661.speaker: Ana Nembe, head of the African Union delegation
